How it works

Bike-share operators publish the status of their stations as an open feed. Station Finder reads it and puts it on a map.

The importer polls the feed

Every minute it fetches the operator's station status feed and keeps the latest state of every station.

The server answers the map

A small JSON API returns the stations in the area you are looking at, plus a history per station.

Your browser draws it

The map app shows a marker per station, coloured by how many bikes it has. Nothing is tracked.

Run it for your city

Station Finder is a Node app with Redis. Point it at your city's station feed and start it with Docker Compose.

git clone https://example.org/station-finder.git cd station-finder cp .env.example .env # set FEED_URL and CITY_NAME docker compose up -d

Then open http://localhost:8700/. See the README for every setting.

Questions

Where does the data come from?

From the bike-share operator's public station feed. Station Finder shows it as published; if the operator's feed is late, so is the map.

How often is it updated?

The importer polls the feed every minute by default. The map refreshes on its own while it is open.

Do you track me?

No. Favourites and filters are stored in your browser only. Your location, if you allow it, never leaves your device.

Why is a station missing?

Stations that stop reporting are hidden after fifteen minutes, so closed or removed stations do not linger on the map.

Can I use the API?

Yes, the JSON API under /api is open. Please keep it under a couple of requests per second.

Does it work for my city?

If your operator publishes a GBFS-style station feed, yes: set FEED_URL and run your own copy.
